title: Fundamentals
summary: The building blocks of English sentences.

lessons.title: Basic sentence structure
lessons.explain: A basic English sentence tells us who or what does something. Most sentences follow the order Subject, then Verb, then Object or other information. The subject comes first, and the verb comes right after it.
structures: Subject + Verb: Birds fly.
Subject + Verb + Object: Maria reads books.
Subject + Verb + Place or Time: We study at home.
positive: My brother works in a bank.
negative: I do not drink coffee.
My brother does not work on Sundays.
questions: Does your brother work in a bank?
reallife: At a cafe: I want a coffee, please.
On the phone: She works until six.

mistakes.why: In English the subject comes before the verb.
The object comes after the verb, not before it.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence has the correct order?
exercises.why: The order is subject (She), verb (reads), object (a book).

exercises.prompt: What is the verb in: Tom plays tennis?
exercises.why: Plays is the action, so it is the verb.
With we, the present form is study.
Subject (Dogs) comes before the verb (bark).

assessment.why: Subject first, then verb, then object.

assessment.prompt: In 'My sister sings songs', which word is the subject?
assessment.why: The sister is the person doing the action.
With they, use play.

assessment.prompt: Which word is the object in: Anna opens the door?
assessment.why: The door receives the action of opening.
Music I like is not the normal order for a basic sentence.

lessons.title: Parts of speech
lessons.explain: Words have different jobs in a sentence. These jobs are called parts of speech. The main ones are noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction and article.
structures: Noun = a person, place or thing: teacher, city, phone.
Verb = an action or state: run, be, think.
Adjective = describes a noun: tall, red. Adverb = describes a verb: quickly, well.
positive: She quickly opened a red door.
Tom and I live in a small town.
negative: The teacher does not speak quickly.
We do not have a big house.
questions: Is your town small or big?
reallife: Shopping: I need a large coffee and a fresh sandwich.
Travel: The train leaves early in the morning.

mistakes.why: Beautifully is an adverb. It describes the verb sings.
An adjective (quick) describes the noun runner.

exercises.why: Happy describes a person or thing.

exercises.prompt: What part of speech is 'slowly' in: He walks slowly?
exercises.why: Slowly tells us how he walks.
Well is the adverb form after a verb.
Jump is an action.

assessment.why: A city is a place, so it is a noun.
And joins words or sentences.
Use the adverb carefully to describe drives.
Sunny is the adjective that describes day.
Pronouns replace nouns. They replaces people or things.

lessons.title: Nouns
lessons.explain: A noun names a person, place, thing or idea. Some nouns can be counted (one book, two books). Some cannot be counted (water, advice, music). Proper nouns are special names and start with a capital letter.
structures: Common noun: a city, a teacher, a car.
Proper noun: London, Maria, Toyota.
Uncountable noun: water, rice, information (no plural).
negative: There is no milk in the fridge.
I do not have any advice.
questions: How many books do you have?
How much water do you drink?
reallife: At the shop: Can I have some rice and two apples?
At work: I need more information about this project.

mistakes.why: Advice is uncountable, so we do not use a or an with it.
Names of cities start with a capital letter.

exercises.prompt: Which word is a proper noun?
exercises.why: Brazil is the name of one particular country.
We say music, not musics.
Water is uncountable and has no plural here.

options: She gave me a good information.
She gave me some good information.
exercises.why: Information is uncountable.

assessment.why: Happiness names an idea or feeling.
Proper nouns and the first word of a sentence need capital letters.

assessment.prompt: We need some ___ for the soup. (rice / a rice)
assessment.why: Rice is uncountable.
We can say one bottle, two bottles.
Bags is countable. Luggage is not.

lessons.title: Pronouns
lessons.explain: A pronoun takes the place of a noun so we do not repeat it. Subject pronouns (I, you, he, she, it, we, they) come before a verb. Object pronouns (me, you, him, her, it, us, them) come after a verb or preposition.
structures: Subject: I, you, he, she, it, we, they + verb.
Object: verb + me, you, him, her, it, us, them.
Possessive: my, your, his, her, its, our, their + noun.
positive: This is my phone, and that is your phone.
negative: He does not know them.
We do not see her.
reallife: At home: Can you help me, please?
Meeting friends: Come with us. We are going to the park.

mistakes.wrong: Me and my friend like football.
mistakes.right: My friend and I like football.
mistakes.why: I is the subject here. Also, it is polite to put the other person first.
After a preposition we use the object form: her.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct word: ___ is my sister.
exercises.why: She is a subject pronoun.

exercises.prompt: I like Tom. I see ___ every day. (he / him)
exercises.why: Him is the object pronoun.
They is the subject pronoun.

exercises.prompt: This is Anna's car. It is ___ car. (she / her)
exercises.why: Her shows the car belongs to Anna.

assessment.why: I is the subject pronoun.

assessment.prompt: Maria and Tom are late. Please call ___. (they / them)
assessment.why: Them is the object pronoun.

assessment.prompt: Which word is a possessive adjective?
assessment.why: Our shows who owns something.
After to, use the object pronoun me.

assessment.prompt: The dog is hungry. ___ wants food. (It / Its)
assessment.why: It is the subject pronoun for an animal or thing.

lessons.title: Verbs
lessons.explain: A verb shows an action (run, eat) or a state (be, have, know). Every sentence needs a verb. The base form is the simple form, like walk or go. In the present simple with he, she or it, we add -s.
structures: Action verb: I walk to work.
State verb: She knows the answer.
Be: I am, you are, he/she/it is, we are, they are.
negative: I do not work on Sundays.
He is not at school.
reallife: Morning routine: I wake up at seven and make coffee.
Introductions: I am a nurse. My friend is a teacher.

mistakes.why: With he, she and it, the present simple verb takes -s or -es.
The verb be changes with the subject: I am.

exercises.why: Dance is an action.
Study becomes studies with he (y changes to ies).
Use are with they.
My mother is she, so add -s.

assessment.why: Verbs that end in -ch add -es.
I am.

assessment.prompt: Which word is a state verb?
assessment.why: Know describes a state of mind, not a physical action.
The children means they, so no -s.
Have becomes has with she.

lessons.title: Adjectives
lessons.explain: An adjective describes a noun. It tells us what something is like: size, colour, age, feeling or opinion. In English the adjective usually comes before the noun, and it does not change for singular or plural.
structures: Adjective + noun: a big house.
Be + adjective: The house is big.
Opinion before fact: a beautiful old house.
positive: They live in a small, quiet town.
negative: The room is not clean.
It is not a cheap hotel.
reallife: In a restaurant: This soup is too salty.
Describing a friend: He is tall, friendly and funny.

mistakes.why: Adjectives do not take a plural -s.
The adjective comes before the noun.

exercises.why: The adjective comes before the noun and does not take -s.
Friendly describes a person.
After be, the adjective describes the subject.
Opinion (beautiful) comes before age (old).

assessment.why: Adjectives do not change for plural.
Red describes the dress.
The adjective comes before the noun.

assessment.prompt: Which word is NOT an adjective?
assessment.why: Slowly is an adverb.
Hot describes the coffee after the verb is.

lessons.title: Adverbs
lessons.explain: An adverb tells us how, when, where or how often something happens. Many adverbs of manner end in -ly (slowly, carefully). Frequency adverbs (always, usually, often, sometimes, never) go before the main verb but after the verb be.
structures: Manner: verb + adverb: She speaks clearly.
Frequency: subject + adverb + verb: I often walk to work.
Frequency with be: He is always late.
positive: I usually have breakfast at eight.
negative: I do not often eat meat.
They do not speak quickly.
reallife: Describing habits: I sometimes cook dinner, but I never wash the dishes.
At work: Please speak slowly. I am learning English.

mistakes.wrong: I go often to the gym.
mistakes.right: I often go to the gym.
mistakes.why: Frequency adverbs usually go before the main verb.
Good is an adjective. Use the adverb well after a verb.

exercises.why: Quietly describes how someone does something.
The adverb goes before the main verb arrives.
With the verb be, the frequency adverb goes after be.
We need an adverb to describe sleeps.

assessment.why: Fast is both an adjective and an adverb. It has no -ly form.
Well is the adverb of good.
Before the main verb.

assessment.prompt: Which adverb tells us HOW OFTEN?
assessment.why: Sometimes shows frequency.

assessment.prompt: They are ___ at home on Sundays. (usually)
assessment.why: After are and before the rest of the sentence.

lessons.title: Articles
lessons.explain: The articles are a, an and the. Use a or an for one thing that is not specific. Use an before a vowel sound (an apple, an hour). Use the when both speaker and listener know which thing we mean. Do not use an article before plural or uncountable nouns in general statements.
structures: a + consonant sound: a book, a university.
an + vowel sound: an egg, an hour.
the + specific thing: Close the door, please.
positive: She eats an apple every day.
negative: I do not have a car.
He is not an engineer.
reallife: At a cafe: I would like a coffee and an orange juice.
Asking directions: Where is the station?

mistakes.why: Engineer begins with a vowel sound, so use an.
For music in general, do not use the.

exercises.why: Orange starts with a vowel sound.
Honest starts with a silent h, so the first sound is a vowel.

exercises.prompt: Please open ___ window. It is hot in here. (a / the)
exercises.why: We know which window, so use the.
General uncountable nouns usually take no article.

assessment.why: University starts with a y sound, a consonant sound.
Umbrella starts with a vowel sound.

assessment.prompt: I saw a film yesterday. ___ film was great. (A / The)
assessment.why: We already mentioned the film, so use the.
Do not use the before the name of a sport.

assessment.prompt: I need ___ hour to finish. (a / an)
assessment.why: Hour begins with a vowel sound.

lessons.title: Determiners
lessons.explain: Determiners come before a noun and tell us which one or how many: a, an, the, this, that, these, those, my, your, his, her, some, any, much, many, few, every, each. A noun usually needs a determiner: we say 'I have a book', not 'I have book'. Use this and these for things near you, and that and those for things far from you. Use many with countable nouns and much with uncountable nouns.
structures: Determiner + noun: this book, my sister, some water
Determiner + adjective + noun: my new phone, those big trees
Much + uncountable noun, many + plural countable noun: much time, many people
negative: I don't have any money.
There isn't much time.
We haven't got many chairs.
questions: How much sugar do you want?
How many brothers have you got?
reallife: In a shop: How much is this shirt? I would like those shoes, please.
At a restaurant: Can I have some more water? Is there any salt?

mistakes.right: I have a lot of water.
mistakes.why: Water is uncountable. Use much or a lot of, not many.
Use this with one thing and these with more than one.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct word: I don't have ___ money.
exercises.why: Money is uncountable, so use much.

exercises.prompt: ___ books on that shelf are mine. (those / that)
exercises.why: Books is plural and far away, so use those.
Every goes with a singular noun and a singular verb.

exercises.prompt: Can I have ___ tea, please? (some / any)
exercises.why: In offers and requests, use some.

assessment.why: People is countable, so use many with are.
Time is uncountable.

assessment.prompt: Which is correct for things that are far away?
assessment.why: Those is the plural of that.

assessment.prompt: ___ person in the room has a ticket. (Every / All)
assessment.why: Every goes with a singular noun: every person.
In negative sentences use any.

lessons.title: Singular and plural
lessons.explain: Singular means one. Plural means more than one. Most nouns add -s (book, books). Nouns ending in s, x, ch or sh add -es (box, boxes). Nouns ending in consonant + y change y to ies (city, cities). Some nouns are irregular (child, children).
structures: Regular: book → books.
Add -es: bus → buses, watch → watches.
Irregular: man → men, woman → women, child → children, foot → feet.
positive: There are three boxes on the table.
I have two brothers and two sisters.
negative: There are not any buses today.
I do not have any children.
questions: How many cities have you visited?
reallife: At the market: I would like two kilos of tomatoes.
At school: There are twenty students in my class.

mistakes.why: Child has an irregular plural.
After a consonant, y changes to ies.

exercises.why: Nouns ending in x add -es.
Woman is irregular.
Consonant + y changes to ies.
Men is the plural of man.

assessment.why: Nouns ending in ch add -es.
Tooth is irregular.
Vowel + y just adds s.
Knife changes to knives.
People is the normal plural of person.

lessons.title: Interjections
lessons.explain: An interjection is a word or short phrase that shows a sudden feeling, such as surprise, pain, joy or disgust. It usually stands alone and is followed by an exclamation mark or a comma: Wow! Oh no! Hurray! Interjections are common in speaking and in informal writing, but they are used less in formal writing.
structures: Interjection + exclamation mark: Wow! That is amazing.
Interjection + comma + sentence: Oh, I forgot my keys.
Interjection as a reaction: Ouch! That hurt.
positive: Oh no! I missed the bus.
negative: Oh no, I haven't finished my homework.
Oops, I didn't mean to say that.
questions: Hey, are you coming with us?
Wow, is this really your house?
reallife: With friends: Hurray! The exam is over! / Ouch! That hurts!
In a shop: Oh, excuse me, do you have this in blue?

mistakes.why: Put an exclamation mark or a comma after an interjection, and end the sentence with a full stop.

mistakes.wrong: Dear Sir, Wow! We received your letter.
mistakes.right: Dear Sir, we received your letter.
mistakes.why: Interjections are informal, so avoid them in formal letters.

exercises.why: Wow shows a sudden feeling.

exercises.prompt: You touch a hot pan. You say: ___! (Ouch / Hurray)
exercises.why: Ouch is used for sudden pain.

options: Oh no! I lost my key.
Oh no I lost my key
Oh no; I lost my key
exercises.why: An exclamation mark (or a comma) follows an interjection.

exercises.prompt: Which interjection fits? We won the match! ___!
exercises.why: Hurray shows joy.

assessment.prompt: Which of these is an interjection?
assessment.why: Hey is a word used to get attention or show surprise.

assessment.prompt: You drop a glass by mistake. You say: ___! (Oops / Hurray)
assessment.why: Oops shows a small mistake.

assessment.prompt: Which sentence is best for a formal business email?
options: Thank you for your quick reply.
assessment.why: Interjections are informal.
Ugh shows that you dislike something.
Hurray shows joy.

lessons.title: Subject and predicate
lessons.explain: Every complete sentence has two parts. The subject is who or what the sentence is about. The predicate says what the subject does or is. It always contains the verb.
structures: Subject + predicate: The old man | walks slowly.
Simple subject = main noun: The old man.
Predicate = verb + rest: walks slowly.
positive: The children | are in the garden.
negative: My neighbour | does not play the piano.
The children | are not in the garden.
questions: Does your neighbour play the piano?
Are the children in the garden?
reallife: Writing an email: The meeting | starts at ten.
News: The train | is late.

mistakes.right: I went home because I was tired.
mistakes.why: The first group of words has no main predicate, so it is not a complete sentence.

mistakes.wrong: The big dog in the garden.
mistakes.right: The big dog is in the garden.
mistakes.why: A sentence needs a verb in the predicate.

exercises.prompt: What is the subject in: The tall boy kicked the ball?
exercises.why: The sentence is about the tall boy.

exercises.prompt: What is the predicate in: Anna sings well?
exercises.why: The predicate contains the verb and what follows.

options: The cat sleeps on the sofa.
exercises.why: It has a subject and a predicate with a verb.

exercises.prompt: The subject of 'My parents live in Delhi' is 'My ___'. (parents)
exercises.why: The sentence is about my parents.

assessment.prompt: What is the subject in: Our new teacher arrived late?
assessment.why: Our new teacher is who the sentence is about.
It has a subject (He) and verb (runs).

assessment.prompt: What is the predicate in: The baby is sleeping?
assessment.why: Is sleeping tells what the baby does.

assessment.prompt: In 'Tom reads books', the verb is '___'. (reads)
assessment.why: The verb is in the predicate.

assessment.prompt: Which group of words is NOT a sentence?
assessment.why: When she arrived does not finish the idea.

lessons.title: Subject-verb agreement
lessons.explain: The verb must agree with the subject. A singular subject (he, she, it, one person or thing) takes a singular verb. A plural subject (we, they, two or more) takes a plural verb. In the present simple, singular verbs end in -s.
structures: Singular: She works. The dog barks.
Plural: They work. The dogs bark.
Be: I am, he is, they are. Have: he has, they have.
negative: My brother does not live in Dubai.
The students are not late.
questions: Does your brother live in Dubai?
reallife: At work: The team meets every Monday.
At home: The keys are on the table.

mistakes.why: Students is plural, so use are.
Everyone is singular.

exercises.prompt: The books ___ on the table. (is / are)
exercises.why: Books is plural.
With she, use doesn't.
My friend is singular, so use has.
Two people means a plural subject.

assessment.why: News is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb.
My sister is singular.
Were goes with they.
Each is singular.
Plural subject, plural verb.

lessons.title: Basic sentence formation
lessons.explain: Now we put everything together. Start with a capital letter, build the sentence with subject, verb and object, add details such as place or time, and finish with a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark. Use and, but, or because to join short sentences.
structures: Subject + verb + object + place + time: I met Sara at the cafe yesterday.
Join ideas: I was tired, but I finished my work.
Reason: I stayed home because it was raining.
positive: I live in Bengaluru, and I work in a school.
We watched a film because it was cold outside.
She likes tea, but he likes coffee.
negative: I do not like spicy food, but my brother does.
She did not go out because she was tired.
questions: Why did you stay at home?
reallife: Introducing yourself: My name is Ravi. I am from Mysuru, and I work as a nurse.
Giving a reason: I am late because the bus was slow.

mistakes.wrong: i am tired but i will finish
mistakes.right: I am tired, but I will finish.
mistakes.why: Start sentences and the word I with a capital letter, and add the final full stop.

mistakes.right: I stayed home because it was raining.
mistakes.why: Because needs a full clause with a subject and verb.

exercises.why: A capital letter at the start and a full stop at the end.

exercises.prompt: I was hungry, ___ I ate a sandwich. (so / because)
exercises.why: So shows the result.

exercises.prompt: Choose the best joining word: I like tea ___ I do not like coffee.
exercises.why: But shows contrast.

exercises.prompt: She stayed at home ___ she was ill. (because)
exercises.why: Because gives the reason.

assessment.why: Capital letter and full stop.

assessment.prompt: He is tall, ___ his brother is short. (but / because)
assessment.why: The two ideas contrast.

options: I went to the market yesterday.
assessment.why: Subject, verb, place, time.

assessment.prompt: We took an umbrella ___ it was raining. (because)
assessment.why: Because gives the reason.

assessment.prompt: Which is a question written correctly?
assessment.why: A question ends with a question mark.
